task.title:
## Product
Story Loom — you write a story opening, and an AI creative partner proposes 
three different directions the story could take (not just one continuation), 
each with a short reason why. You pick one, it becomes a node on a visual 
tree, and you can branch again from ANY earlier node, not just the latest — 
so the whole story becomes an explorable tree, not a scrolling document.

## Core user flow
1. User types an opening (1-3 sentences) into a text box.
2. On submit, call the AI to generate exactly 3 branch options. Each option 
   has: continuation text (1-3 sentences), a tone tag (single word, e.g. 
   "Tense"), and a one-line rationale ("Why: raises the stakes...").
3. Render these as 3 cards below the parent node, connected by a line.
4. Clicking a card commits it as a new node; the path from root to it is 
   visually highlighted.
5. Clicking any existing node (not just the newest) re-triggers step 2 
   branching from that node, growing the tree sideways.
6. A "Read this path" button stitches the highlighted root-to-node path 
   into a single clean block of story text.

## Tech stack
- Frontend: React + Tailwind, using react-flow (or similar) for the node/tree 
  canvas, since it handles pan/zoom/node layout for us.
- Backend: Node.js (or Python/Flask) exposing one endpoint: given the current 
  path text, return 3 branch options as JSON.
- AI: call watsonx/Granite (or whichever LLM Bob has configured) with a 
  system prompt instructing it to output ONLY valid JSON: an array of 3 
  objects with keys "text", "tone", "why".

## Non-negotiables
- No login/dashboard shell — the tree canvas IS the whole app.
- Every branch generation must include the "why" rationale, visibly shown 
  on the card — this is the "creative partner" element, don't drop it.
- Branching must work from ANY node, not just the most recent one.

## Explicitly out of scope for v1
- No user accounts or auth
- No saving/loading across sessions (single in-memory session is fine)
- No illustrations/images per node (add only if time remains)
- No audio narration (add only if time remains)

# Create Plan

Follow this structured workflow to produce a high-quality, actionable plan.

## Step 1 — Gather Requirements

Ask the user clarifying questions to fully understand the task:
- What is the goal and expected outcome?
- Are there constraints, preferences, or non-goals?
- Which parts of the codebase are likely involved?
- Any related issues or requirement documents?

Do not proceed until you have enough context to scope the work, be critical of vague intent or requirements.

## Step 2 — Code Search via Sub-Agent

Spawn a `spawn_subagent` of type `"explore"` to research the codebase. The sub-agent should:
- Locate relevant files, symbols, and patterns related to the task
- Identify existing utilities or abstractions that should be reused
- Identify existing design patterns
- Surface any constraints or conventions (e.g. patterns in similar files)

Use the sub-agent's findings to ground your plan in the actual code.

## Step 3 — Clarify Design Intention

Based on the requirements and code research:
- Always confirm your understanding of the intended design with the user
- Raise any open questions or trade-offs that need a decision
- Adjust scope if the code research revealed complexity or simplifications

Do not begin writing the plan document until design intent is confirmed.

## Step 4 — Write the Plan File

Write a structured plan to a markdown file (e.g. `{short-plan-name}-plan.md`). The plan must NOT go into low-level code detail — focus on *what* needs to happen and *why*.

The plan file must include:

### Top-Level Overview
A concise summary of the goal, scope, and approach.

### Sub-Tasks
Break the work into sub-tasks. Each sub-task must have:
- **Intent** — what this sub-task achieves and why
- **Expected Outcomes** — observable results when this sub-task is complete
- **Todo List** — ordered, specific steps to achieve the outcome
- **Relevant Context** — pointers to relevant files, symbols, or patterns
- **Status** — `[ ] pending` (updated to `[x] done` after completion)

Design each sub-task to be processed independently, one at a time, so changes stay focused and reviewable.

## Step 5 — Plan Validation

Before moving to implementation, ensure that the user has fully read the plan. Always ask the user targeted questions to verify the plan is correct and complete:
- Does this plan capture the full scope of the task?
- Are the sub-task boundaries and ordering correct?
- Is any context missing that would be needed during implementation?

Use Mermaid diagrams in chat responses where they clarify architecture or workflow, but do not place Mermaid diagrams directly in the plan file. Avoid double quotes and parentheses inside square brackets in Mermaid syntax.

Refine the plan file based on the user's answers.

## Step 6 — Implementation

Only after the user confirms the plan, recommend implementation by calling the `switch_mode` tool to `agent`.

When explaining how to implement the plan in agent mode:
- Using the `start_subtask` tool, create a new task for each subtask in the <plan-file>.
- In the prompt for the subtask make sure it reads the plan-file to gain the full context around the task.
- After each sub task is complete update the task status in the <plan-file>
- Add any context needed for the next subtask in the <plan-file>
- Wait for the user to check and ok the changes before moving on to the next subtask.

## Reminders

- Ask questions always using the "ask_followup_question" tool
- Never include information without evidence
- Don't include time estimates
Now let me explore the existing codebase to understand what's already there before asking clarifying questions.

The caller may specify a thoroughness level: "quick", "medium", or "thorough".
- quick: 1-2 targeted searches, return immediately
- medium: explore a few related files, follow one level of references
- thorough: check multiple locations, naming conventions, and related patterns
If no level is specified, default to "medium".

Tools (use in this order of preference):
1. grep — search file contents by regex pattern. Use this first to find relevant code.
2. glob — find files by name pattern (e.g. "**/*.ts"). Use to locate files.
3. read_file with range — read specific line ranges only. NEVER read entire files.
4. list_files — list directory contents. Use sparingly.
5. read_file without range — only as a last resort when you need full file context.

Example workflow:
  grep pattern="handleAuth" → finds src/auth.ts line 42
  read_file path="src/auth.ts" range="38-60" → read only the relevant function
  grep pattern="handleAuth" include="*.test.ts" → find related tests
Do NOT: read_file path="src/auth.ts" (without range) — this wastes tokens on irrelevant code.

Strategy:
- Start narrow: grep/glob first, then read only what's relevant
- Call multiple tools in parallel when possible
- When reading files, request specific line ranges — never read entire files
- Expand scope only if initial searches don't answer the question
- Stop as soon as you have enough context

Do not explain code, suggest changes, or give opinions.

- File paths and line numbers of relevant code

The plan is written. Here's a review summary for you:

## Story Loom — Plan Summary

The plan is in [`story-loom-plan.md`](story-loom-plan.md). Here's the architecture at a glance:

```mermaid
graph TD
    A[app/page.tsx\nuseReducer + orchestration] --> B[components/StoryTree.tsx\nReact Flow canvas]
    A --> C[components/BranchPanel.tsx\n3 branch cards]
    A --> D[POST /api/generate-branches\nroute.ts]
    D --> E[lib/ai/generateBranches.ts\nSTUB - swap for watsonx here]
    B --> F[components/StoryNodeCard.tsx\ncustom React Flow node]
    A --> G[lib/treeUtils.ts\ngetPath / pathToText / computeLayout]
    A --> H[lib/types.ts\nBranchOption / StoryNode / TreeState]
```

**7 sub-tasks in order:**

| # | Sub-Task | What it produces |
|---|----------|-----------------|
| 1 | Project Scaffold | Next.js + Tailwind + React Flow setup, `npm run dev` works |
| 2 | Data Model & State | `lib/types.ts` + `lib/treeUtils.ts` — pure types and layout math |
| 3 | API Route | `/api/generate-branches` + stubbed `generateBranches()` function |
| 4 | Tree Canvas | `StoryTree` + `StoryNodeCard` — React Flow with custom nodes and highlighted path |
| 5 | Branch Panel | `BranchPanel` — 3 cards with tone, text, "Why:" rationale, loading skeletons |
| 6 | Main Page Wiring | Full `useReducer` state machine connecting everything end-to-end |
| 7 | Polish & README | Visual touches, watsonx swap comment, build check |

**Key decisions captured:**
- `generateBranches(pathText)` in [`lib/ai/generateBranches.ts`](story-loom-plan.md) is the **single swap point** for watsonx — one function, clearly commented.
- `WATSONX_API_KEY` / `WATSONX_PROJECT_ID` live only in `.env.local` — never client-side.
- State shape (`TreeState`) is defined up-front so all 7 sub-tasks share the same contract.

**Three questions to confirm before we proceed:**

1. **Node click behavior:** When you click a node that *already has children*, should it re-generate fresh branches (potentially different suggestions) or show the existing children as the options panel? The plan currently re-generates fresh — is that right?

2. **"Read this path" display:** The plan uses a simple modal overlay. Would you prefer it as a side-drawer, or an inline expandable section below the branch panel instead?

3. **Root node handling:** The opening text becomes the root node (tone = "Opening", no why). Should the opening textarea disappear entirely once the root is committed, or stay accessible in a collapsed/minimized state?

# Story Loom

An AI-powered collaborative story branching tool. Write an opening, receive three AI-generated directions the story could take (each with a rationale), pick one — and branch again from any node in the tree, not just the latest.

## Quick start

```bash
npm install
npm run dev
```

Open [http://localhost:3000](http://localhost:3000).

## How to use

1. **Write your opening** in the text box and press **Begin story** (or ⌘ Enter).
2. Three branch cards appear at the bottom — each shows a continuation, a tone badge, and a **Why:** rationale.
3. **Click a card** to commit it as a new node. The root-to-node path highlights in amber.
4. **Three interaction modes from any node on the canvas:**
   - **Click the node body** — if it already has children, those children reappear as the branch panel (no API call). If it has no children, it just selects the node and updates the active path.
   - **Click "＋ New directions"** inside a node — always generates a fresh set of AI branch options for that node, regardless of existing children.
   - **Click a branch card** — commits the chosen option as a new child node.
5. **Read this path** (top-right button) slides open a drawer with the full story from root to the selected node. Use **Copy** to grab the text.
6. **✏ Edit opening** (top-right, after the tree starts) re-expands the opening textarea. Re-submitting will show a confirmation banner before clearing the tree.

## Wiring watsonx / Granite AI

The branch generation is currently stubbed with hardcoded mock data in [`lib/ai/generateBranches.ts`](lib/ai/generateBranches.ts). To wire the real model:

1. Install the IBM watsonx AI SDK:
   ```bash
   npm install @ibm-cloud/watsonx-ai
   ```

2. Copy `.env.local.example` to `.env.local` and fill in your credentials:
   ```
   WATSONX_API_KEY=<your IAM API key>
   WATSONX_PROJECT_ID=<your watsonx project id>
   ```

3. Open `lib/ai/generateBranches.ts` and follow the **STEP 1 / 2 / 3** comments at the top — the full replacement implementation is included there as a code comment, ready to uncomment.

The API key is only ever read server-side (inside the Next.js API route `/api/generate-branches`) — it is never sent to the browser.

## Project structure

```
app/
  page.tsx                  Main page — useReducer state machine, all UI assembly
  layout.tsx                Root HTML shell
  globals.css               Tailwind + React Flow base styles
  api/generate-branches/

  PathDrawer.tsx            Right-side drawer — story path text + Copy button

lib/
  types.ts                  TypeScript interfaces: BranchOption, StoryNode, TreeState
  treeUtils.ts              Pure utilities: getPath, pathToText, computeLayout
  ai/
    generateBranches.ts     Stubbed AI function — swap point for watsonx
```

## Tech stack

- [Next.js 14](https://nextjs.org) (App Router, TypeScript)
- [React Flow (@xyflow/react)](https://reactflow.dev) — canvas, pan/zoom, edges
- [Tailwind CSS](https://tailwindcss.com)
